title: A last poem
hookLine: Japanese monks and poets wrote a short poem as death approached

cards: A brush, a sheet of paper, and not much time. In Japan, Zen monks and poets kept a custom: as death came near, they would leave a short poem behind. It was called a jisei, a farewell poem.
Not a will, not a speech, not a list of regrets. Sometimes just a picture: a field, a moon, a sound in the night. What does someone choose to see when they know they're writing the last thing?

teach.b: First, the custom. A farewell poem was a way of meeting death with attention instead of only fear. Tradition says some Zen teachers were expected to leave a verse for their students, a last teaching in a handful of words.
Poets took up the practice too. Second, a sickbed. The poet Matsuo Bashō walked the roads of Japan and wrote about them.
He fell ill on a journey, and his students wrote down a poem from those days.
In plain English, it says something like: sick on a journey, my dreams go wandering over withered fields. That's it. No lesson about death.
Just a traveler who, lying still, is still traveling in his dreams, across a winter landscape. Third, a story people tell.
When his students asked for a death poem, the story goes, Bashō answered that every poem he had written was his death poem.
Whether or not he said it, the idea has stayed: if any poem might be the last, each one is written with that care. Fourth, why it matters on a Tuesday.
A last poem asks: if there were only a few words left, what would be worth seeing?

The answer can be small, the way Bashō's was: a field, gone brown, and a traveler's dream crossing it. Writing one long before the end isn't gloomy. It's a way of finding out what you notice when you stop to look.

how: In Japan, Zen monks and poets kept a custom of writing a short farewell poem, a jisei, as death approached; these poems are still collected, read and written today.

practice: Make a three-line poem under your breath, no counting syllables, no rhyme.
Look at one thing in front of you or listen to one sound: let the first line name it, the second say what it's doing, the third add one surprise, or simply where you are.
Say it to yourself a few times, and change a word if one feels wrong.

wordCard.voice: Jisei: a Japanese farewell poem, written by monks and poets as death drew near, sometimes about something small seen clearly. Today's word.

orig.note: Japanese: jisei, the word for a farewell poem left at the end of life.
